messages.subject: Advice on Hierarchical Model
parts:
This is a follow-up to my previous posts (hopefully the last one)! Previous posts:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Lindsay/stan-users/fsM8GPG4cpM/T09Y38Rx3MMJ
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Lindsay/stan-users/fsM8GPG4cpM/T09Y38Rx3MMJ

I am getting to the edge of my statistical knowledge, here, so my question is really of two parts (1) how can I get this to work; and (2) is it even sensible.

I am working on budgetary data. To recap, data are expenditure data, and I have 71 agencies over four years (actually five years, but the data is differenced). Agencies are further divided into agency types. The goal is to see whether different types of agencies followed different trajectories over the short time period. I got the following model to run just fine, and the results make sense.

hier_1 <- "data {
                int<lower=1> N_obs;
                int<lower=1> N_agencies;
                int<lower=1> N_years;
                int <lower=1, upper=N_agencies> agency[N_obs];
                int <lower=1, upper=N_years> year[N_obs];
                real y[N_obs];
                int <lower=1> N_types;
                int <lower=1, upper=N_types> type[N_agencies];
   
                }
                            
            parameters {
                real a_agency[N_agencies];
                real b_year[N_years];
                real<lower=0, upper=500> sigma[N_agencies];
                real a_type[N_types];
                real <lower=0, upper=500> sigma_a[N_types];
                            }
            
            transformed parameters{

                             }
                     
            model {
                    vector[N_obs] y_hat;
                    vector[N_agencies] mu_a;
                   
                    a_type ~ normal(0, 100);
                    
                    for(j in 1:N_agencies){
                        mu_a[j] <- a_type[type[j]];
                        a_agency[j] ~ normal(mu_a[j], sigma_a[type[j]]);
                    }
                
                    
                    b_year ~ normal(0, 100);

                    for(i in 1:N_obs){
                                       y_hat[i] <- a_agency[agency[i]] + b_year[year[i]];
                                      y[i] ~ normal(y_hat[i], sigma[agency[i]]);             
                                    }    
                              
                                   
               
                                }"

What I would like to do now is to allow the parameter a_type to vary by year. The right hand panel of the following graph (which was done by running a few linear models in R and thenrunning linear models on the coefficients) shows what I am aiming for, roughly speaking:



What I would like to do now is therefore to allow the parameter a_type (and hence logically a_agency) to vary by year.  The best I can think of is something like the following:

stan_data <- list("y"=y,
                  "year"=year,
                  "N_years"=N_years,
                  "agency"=agency,
                  "N_agencies" = N_agencies,
                  "N_obs" = N_obs,
                  "type" = type,
                  "N_types" = N_types)

hier_1 <- "data {
                int<lower=1> N_obs;
                int<lower=1> N_agencies;
                int<lower=1> N_years;
                int <lower=1, upper=N_agencies> agency[N_obs];
                int <lower=1, upper=N_years> year[N_obs];
                real y[N_obs];
                int <lower=1> N_types;
                int <lower=1, upper=N_types> type[N_agencies];
   
                }
                           
            parameters {
                matrix[N_agencies, N_years] a_agency;
                real b_year[N_years];
                real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_y[N_agencies];
                matrix[N_types, N_years] a_type;
                real <lower=0, upper=100> sigma_a[N_types];
                real <lower=0, upper=100> sigma_state[N_types];
                            }
             
            transformed parameters{

                             }
                      
            model {
                    vector[N_obs] y_hat;
                    matrix[N_agencies, N_years] mu_a;
                                  
   
                    for(j in 1:N_agencies){
                        a_type[[type[j],1] ~ normal(0, 100);
                       
                        for(t in 2:N_years){
                                        a_type[type[j],t] ~ normal(a_type[type[j],t-1], sigma_state[type[j]]);
                                            }   
                       
                        for(t in 1:N_years){
                                        mu_a[j,t] <- a_type[type[j],t];
                                        a_agency[j,t] ~ normal(mu_a[j,t], sigma_a[type[j]]);
                                            }
                               
                                        }

                    for(i in 1:N_obs){
                        for(t in 1:N_years){
                                       y_hat[i] <- a_agency[agency[i],t];
                                  }
                                      y[i] ~ normal(y_hat[i], sigma_y[agency[i]]);            
                                    }   
                                   
                                   
                             
            }"

This blows up, when I try to run it. The error message (below) is I think not helpful. I'd appreciate any advice on where I am going wrong, as well as, as I said, whether this is a sensible approach. Also, thanks for your patience with repeated queries as I try to get to know STAN.

Thanks in advance.

Lindsay

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Advice on Hierarchical Model
parts:
The segfault you saw in the previous message should never
happen. If it does, it's either a bug in our code (most likely)
or a corruption of memory in the hardware (less likely).

So I'm glad you're not seeing it in 1.2.0.

The main places segfaults can creep in is if we don't properly
allocate an array or test its bounds during access, or if we
don't properly allocate a parameter, transformed parameter,
or local variable in a model.

As to the model itself, the basic idea looks OK at first
glance. And fitting simpler models first is absolutely the
right way to go. But this looks wrong:

for(j in 1:N_agencies)
a_type[[type[j],1] ~ normal(0, 100);

You almost certainly want to sample a_type in a loop over the types,
like this:

for (t in 1:N_types)
a_type[t,1] ~ normal(0,100);

As is, you are implicitly specifying the prior as a product
of normal(0,100) distributions, one for each agency with the
given type. This is legal syntax in Stan, but BUGS would flag
it as illegal.

The same goes for the rest of the time series. So you want
to break this out into two loops --- one for a_type, and one
for a_agency.

I suggest (1) applying a transform to the normals (aka the
Matt trick, as described in the manual), and (2)
vectorizing. (1) should speed convergence, and (2) should
speed up each iteration.

Also, if you can provide sensible initial values it'll help
for regressions with lots of parameters. Or try initializing
to 0 to see if that helps get at least one chain toward its
destination.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Advice on Hierarchical Model
parts:
Not quite. You need to keep everything connected.
Your model requires an independent looping for each level
in a multilevel model and then one for the regression
itself.

Though I haven't really tried to understand your model,
the looping required would be something like this:

for (k in 1:N_types) {
a_type[k,1] ~ normal(0,100);
for (t in 2:N_years)

a_type[k,t] ~ normal(a_type[k,t-1], sigma_state[k]);
}

for (j in 1:N_agencies)
for (t in 1:N_years)
a_agency[j,t] ~ normal(a_type[type[j],t],
sigma_a[type[j]]);

You're assuming a very fat uniform prior in [0,100]
on sigma_a and sigma_state. You might want to limit that
a bit more if you deviations of 100 don't make sense.

Your last loop also looks wrong:

for(i in 1:N_obs) {
for(t in 1:N_years) {
y_hat[i] <- a_agency[agency[i],t];
}
y[i] ~ normal(y_hat[i], sigma_y[agency[i]]);
}

I'm not sure what you meant here, but you're setting
y_hat a total of N_years time in the inner loop and then
only using the last one. The t parameter isn't in scope for
your model of y[i], so I'm not sure where it's coming from.

- Bob

I would like to further impose on the good-will of this group with one further question---one which perhaps relates to the substance of my modelling problem than the use of Stan. At the same time, I wouldn't put it past me to have made a basic error in trying to express my modelling ideas in code.

I think I have written a model which represents the substance of my problem. I gave budgetary data observations nested in agencies, which are in turn nested within agency types. Agency type is allowed to vary by year (and so hence do the lower-levels which take a value according to agency type). The model (shown below) seems to converge pretty within about 10000 iterations. The problem is that the credible intervals seem too narrow (shown in the graph below, which plots also the data). I get the concept of "shrinkage" in Bayesian models but this seems excessive! The variance of the sigmas is pretty large, but if I make it any smaller, the estimates seem to "bump up" against the upper limit of the sampling. In any case the variability in the data is pretty huge. When I set what I consider reasonable inits for a_type[k, 1], I don't seem to do any better than when I allow Stan defaults to do the work.

So I guess the questions are (in order): (1) am I doing something stupid, so that my code doesn't represent the model I want to run? (2) is there anything I can do, like changing priors? (3) Could it be that the sampler is not exploring the extremes of the distribution very effectively? On this last point, it doesn't seem to make a difference if I run a million iterations, and thin every 200 over the last 500000. It occurs to me that maybe the time-dependence structure I am imposing by the t in 2:N_years loop may be too restrictive, but I am not sure what alternatives to try.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Advice on Hierarchical Model
parts:
On 3/21/13 6:08 AM, Lindsay wrote:
...

I found the original post -- don't know why I didn't see it
earlier.

First, modeling. Are the zeroes really zeroes and not
missing data? If they're missing data, you should model
the missingness rather than just including them in the
data. If they're real, I'm not sure a simple regression is the
right model, because the data looks more like a mixture of zeroes
and a real trend.

Although you seem to be able to run 1M iterations (!!!), the
model can be made more efficient in two ways. Here are the
original loops:

mu_a_type1 ~ normal(5000, 100);
for (k in 1:N_types) {
a_type[k,1] ~ normal(mu_a_type1, sd_a_type1);
for (t in 2:N_years)

a_type[k,t] ~ normal(a_type[k,t-1], sigma_state[k]);
}

Nice use of naming conventions, by the way -- I could understand
the model just by reading it.

To speed up the iterations without changing the model, you
can vectorize. If you let a_type_tr be the transpose of a_type,
you can write the above loops in vectorized form as:

a_type_tr[1] ~ normal(mu_a_type1, sd_a_type1);
for (t in 2:N_years)

a_type_tr[t] ~ normal(a_type_tr[t-1], sigma_state);

The vectorized versions are a lot faster. If N_types is
small, the gains will be modest. You could even go a step
further and vectorize the second call to normal by defining
a temporary. It's the calls to normal that are slow, not
looping or assignments, and vectorizing speeds up the calls
to normal.

By using the "Matt trick", you can also speed up sampling in
terms of number of effective samples per iteration. Working
from the vectorized code above, the Matt-ed out code would involve
a new raw parameter and would move a_type_tr to a transformed
parameter, with model code:

a_type_tr_raw[1] ~ normal(0,1);
for (k in 1:N_types)

a_type_tr_raw[t] ~ normal(0,1);

and transformed parameter code:

a_type_tr[1] <- a_type_tr_raw[1] * sd_a_type1 + mu_a_type1;
for (t in 2:N_years)

a_type_tr[t] <- a_type_tr_raw[t] * sd_a_type1 + a_type_tr[t-1];

You'd then use a_type_tr as before.

Having said all this, I really don't want to encourage people
to prematurely optimize. If the model's already fast enough
to converge and sample once it converges, I wouldn't change it!

But if you want to do more groups or handle lots more data, the
above can really help.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Advice on Hierarchical Model
parts:
Dear Stan Users,

Two resolutions (of sorts) and one further query.

As Daniel Lee figured out, I was sampling from the unobserved mean parameter, when I wanted the predictive distribution. It was of course easy to add the following line to my code:

    a_type_predict[k, t] ~ normal (a_type[k, t], sigma_state[k]);

The zeros are definitely zeros rather than missing; Bob Carpenter's suggestion of a mixture is intriguing, but is something I am going to have to look into in the meantime.

Finally, when I add the following code block to my code, Stan crashes---sometimes mid-way through sampling. Sometimes I get a segfault error and I am asked to shut R down, sometimes R just shuts down. Can anyone help explain this?

            transformed parameters{
                matrix [N_types, N_years] exp_a_type;
                matrix [N_types, N_years-1] delta_exp_a_type;
                        for(k in 1:N_types){
                            for(t in 1:N_years){
                                    exp_a_type[k,t] <- exp(a_type[k,t]);
                                        }
                            for(t in 2:N_years){
                            delta_exp_a_type[k,t] <- exp_a_type[k,t] - exp_a_type[k, t-1];
                            }
                        }           
                    }

It is the line delta_exp_a_type[k,t] <- exp_a_type[k,t] - exp_a_type[k, t-1]; that seems to do the damage. There is nothing in the values of exp_a_type that seem to suggest that that this should be a problem.

Lindsay

Yikes. Stan shouldn't be crashing with a segfault.
I'm going to investigate where that's still happening.

The problem in your code is that you declare

> matrix [N_types, N_years-1] delta_exp_a_type;

then loop

> for (t in 2:N_years) {
> delta_exp_a_type[k,t] <- exp_a_type[k,t] - exp_a_type[k, t-1];

When t= N_years, it overruns the matrix delta_exp_a_type in
the second index.

- Bob
